Platform/MASTG-TEST0007.title: Determining Whether Sensitive Stored Data Has Been Exposed via IPC Mechanisms

expected_vulnerabilities.description: The app exposes a ContentProvider that allows other apps to access sensitive stored data through IPC.
The ContentProvider query logic is vulnerable to SQL injection through attacker-controlled selection/query input.

Platform/MASTG-TEST0007.notes: This case is evaluated as a Platform/IPC security issue. Extra findings such as vulnerable minSdk, logging, hardcoded strings, or third-party library issues are not the target ground truth for this benchmark.

Platform/MASTG-TEST0008.title: Checking for Sensitive Data Disclosure Through the User Interface

expected_vulnerabilities.description: The app asks for sensitive values such as credit card number and PIN, but the input fields are not obscured during entry.
The app sends a notification that contains the credit card number and PIN in plaintext.

Platform/MASTG-TEST0008.notes: This case targets sensitive data exposure through UI and notifications. A scanner may need both layout XML analysis and source-level dataflow to detect both findings.

Platform/MASTG-TEST0024.title: Testing for App Permissions

expected_vulnerabilities.description: The camera app requests permissions that are not necessary for its core functionality of taking photos and saving them to internal storage.
The app requests dangerous permissions such as phone, contacts, and calendar permissions without clear need.
expected_vulnerabilities.source: README.md Android Permissions and Permission Analysis

Platform/MASTG-TEST0024.notes: This case is evaluated as an over-permission issue. Runtime permission handling problems may be reported as extra findings, but the core target is that the app requests permissions unrelated to the app purpose.

Platform/MASTG-TEST0028.title: Testing Deep Links

expected_vulnerabilities.description: The app exposes deep links through exported intent filters, increasing the attack surface and allowing external intents to reach app functionality.
expected_vulnerabilities.source: README.md Check for Deep Link Usage

expected_vulnerabilities.description: The app login can be bypassed by generating a crafted intent from the terminal through the deep link entry point.
expected_vulnerabilities.source: README.md Implementation and Check the Handler Method

expected_vulnerabilities.description: Externally controlled deep link parameters can modify the content or URL displayed inside a WebView.
expected_vulnerabilities.source: README.md Implementation and Check the Handler Method

Platform/MASTG-TEST0028.notes: This case targets deep link attack surface and deep-link-controlled WebView behavior. Asset Links verification issues can be extra findings, but the main benchmark target is externally reachable deep link abuse.

Platform/MASTG-TEST0030.title: Testing for Vulnerable Implementation of PendingIntent

expected_vulnerabilities.description: The app creates a PendingIntent using the MUTABLE flag, allowing the intent to be modified after creation.
The base intent used by the PendingIntent is implicit or not restricted to an exact package, action, and component.

Platform/MASTG-TEST0030.notes: This case targets unsafe PendingIntent construction. A scanner should ideally detect both the mutable PendingIntent and the unsafe implicit base Intent.

Platform/MASTG-TEST0031.title: Testing JavaScript Execution in WebViews

expected_vulnerabilities.description: The app explicitly enables JavaScript execution in a WebView.
The app takes a user search query from an EditText and loads related results into a WebView, making WebView content influenced by user input.

Platform/MASTG-TEST0031.notes: JavaScript enabled is not always a vulnerability by itself. In this benchmark, it is treated as vulnerable because the WebView loads content based on user-provided input.

Platform/MASTG-TEST0032.title: Testing WebView Protocol Handlers

expected_vulnerabilities.description: The app loads an HTML file from external storage into a WebView, allowing other apps or users to overwrite the loaded content.
The WebView may allow file/content access or does not explicitly disable risky protocol handlers.
The network security configuration permits cleartext traffic for 10.0.2.2.

Platform/MASTG-TEST0032.notes: This case targets WebView protocol-handler misuse, especially loading attacker-modifiable files from external storage. Cleartext traffic is included because it is explicitly part of the case setup.

Platform/MASTG-TEST0033.title: Testing for Java Objects Exposed Through WebViews

expected_vulnerabilities.description: The app exposes a Java object to JavaScript through addJavascriptInterface.
JavaScript is enabled in a WebView that also exposes a JavaScript bridge.
The activity containing the WebView bridge is exported or externally reachable, increasing exploitability.

Platform/MASTG-TEST0033.notes: This case targets WebView JavaScript bridge exposure. The secret string behavior is useful evidence, but the core scanner target is addJavascriptInterface combined with JavaScript and external reachability.

Platform/MASTG-TEST0035.title: Testing for Overlay Attacks

expected_vulnerabilities.description: Sensitive UI elements do not enable touch filtering protections against overlay or tapjacking attacks.
The app does not implement custom touch security checks such as onFilterTouchEventForSecurity or checks for obscured touch flags.

Platform/MASTG-TEST0035.notes: The SYSTEM_ALERT_WINDOW permission belongs to the exploit/malicious overlay app in the scenario. The victim-app ground truth is mainly missing overlay/tapjacking defenses on sensitive UI.

Platform/MASTG-TEST0037.title: Testing WebViews Cleanup

expected_vulnerabilities.description: The app uses WebView storage-related features or may store WebView data without properly deleting WebStorage data.
The app does not fully clear WebView cache, or does not call clearCache with disk-file cleanup.
The app does not remove cookies stored by WebView during cleanup.
The app does not manually delete known WebView data directories such as app_webview.
expected_vulnerabilities.source: README.md File APIs and Static Analysis

Platform/MASTG-TEST0037.notes: This case targets incomplete cleanup of WebView data. Some cleanup checks are absence-based, so scanners may report them as missing best practices rather than directly proven exploitable vulnerabilities.

Network/MASTG-TEST0019.title: Testing Data Encryption on the Network

expected_vulnerabilities.description: The app makes network requests to plain HTTP URLs instead of HTTPS, exposing transmitted data to interception or modification.
The AndroidManifest.xml explicitly enables cleartext traffic by setting android:usesCleartextTraffic="true" in the application tag.
The app skips hostname verification, which can allow man-in-the-middle attackers to present certificates for the wrong host.
The app disables TLS or SSL error handling, allowing connections to proceed even when certificate validation fails.
The app uses a low minimum SDK version, minSdk = 19, which can weaken or bypass protections expected from newer Android network security defaults.
The app explicitly uses an outdated TLS protocol version, TLS 1.0, for HTTPS connections. Obsolete TLS versions are insecure and should be replaced with modern versions such as TLS 1.2 or TLS 1.3.
The app disables SSL/TLS certificate validation by installing a custom TrustManager that trusts all certificates, including self-signed or expired certificates.

The app targets Android API level 23, which is lower than 24. Apps targeting below Android 7.0 do not benefit from the newer default Network Security Configuration behavior that avoids trusting user-supplied CAs by default.
The app may trust user-provided certificate authorities through insecure Network Security Configuration trust anchors, allowing malicious user-installed CAs to intercept TLS traffic.

The app ignores TLS certificate errors in WebView by overriding onReceivedSslError and calling handler.proceed(), allowing the WebView to continue loading pages even when certificate validation fails.

The app disables hostname verification by using a HostnameVerifier that always returns true, allowing TLS connections to succeed even when the server certificate does not match the requested hostname.

The app lacks proper certificate validation through TrustManager or may use an insecure TrustManager pattern that accepts certificates without checking whether they are trusted, expired, or self-signed.

Network/MASTG-TEST0022.title: Testing Custom Certificate Stores and Certificate Pinning

expected_vulnerabilities.description: The app includes a network request path that connects to www.example.com without certificate pinning, making the connection more exposed to interception if a malicious or user-installed CA is trusted.

The app implements certificate pinning through Network Security Configuration. The scanner should identify the presence of pinning-related configuration such as pin-set entries and extract relevant evidence for review.
If the app defines certificate pinning with an expired pin-set, certificate pinning will be disabled for the affected domains. This should be reported when an expired pin-set is found.

The app may use a custom certificate store or KeyStore-based TrustManager for certificate pinning. The scanner should recognize KeyStore, TrustManagerFactory, and SSLContext usage as pinning-related evidence rather than automatically treating it as insecure.
If the app uses OkHttp, certificate pinning may be implemented through OkHttp CertificatePinner. The scanner should recognize CertificatePinner configuration as certificate-pinning evidence.

The app does not update the Android security provider through Google Play Services ProviderInstaller. Without updating the provider, the app may continue using an outdated TLS/SSL implementation that is vulnerable to known SSL/TLS issues.

The app does not include the Google Play Services dependency required for using ProviderInstaller, such as com.google.android.gms:play-services-gcm. As a result, the app cannot perform the recommended security provider update checks.

If the app attempts to update the security provider, exceptions from ProviderInstaller should be caught and handled correctly. The app should report the insecure state to the backend or restrict risky user actions if the provider cannot be patched.

If the app uses NDK-based networking or native TLS libraries, the scanner should identify native SSL/TLS library usage so reviewers can verify that it binds only to recent and properly patched SSL/TLS implementations.

The app performs login checks against a local SQL database without properly sanitizing or parameterizing user input. An attacker can use SQL injection payloads such as ' or 1=1 -- - to bypass authentication.
The app does not validate user-controlled input before using it in security-sensitive logic. Input validation should be applied to UI input, IPC input, and URL scheme input before processing.
If the app exposes a ContentProvider that builds SQL queries from URI path segments or other IPC-controlled input, other apps may be able to trigger SQL injection through the provider.
The app should use prepared statements or parameterized queries instead of concatenating user-controlled input into SQL statements.
The app uses an implicit intent action for sensitive functionality, allowing another app that registers the same action with higher priority to intercept the intent flow.

The app exposes sensitive post-login functionality, adding a credit card, through an intent-based flow. If the intent is not explicit or otherwise protected, another app may intercept or abuse the flow.
If the app uses startActivityForResult with an implicit intent and does not validate the returned URI or result data, an attacker-controlled app may return malicious file:// or content:// URIs.
Improper validation of an implicit intent return URI can allow a malicious app to cause arbitrary files from the victim app's internal storage to be copied to externally readable storage.

Improper handling of file:// or content:// URLs returned from an implicit intent can enable arbitrary code execution when attacker-controlled native libraries or files are copied and loaded by the victim app.

Code/MASTG-TEST0027.title: Testing for URL Loading in WebViews

expected_vulnerabilities.description: The app disables WebView Safe Browsing by setting android.webkit.WebView.EnableSafeBrowsing to false in the AndroidManifest.xml file.

The app handles page navigation inside a WebView without adequately validating URLs, allowing users or attackers to navigate away from trusted content and potentially load phishing pages or malicious content.
The app overrides shouldOverrideUrlLoading and handles all URL loading inside the WebView without proper allowlist or scheme validation.
The app overrides shouldInterceptRequest and returns crafted responses based on weak string matching instead of robust URL validation, which may allow content injection or security check bypasses.

When a WebViewClient handles navigation and resource interception, the app should validate URL schemes such as http, https, data, file, and content. Failure to restrict schemes may allow unexpected local file or injected content loading.
The app does not implement an enforced update mechanism or version check to prevent users from continuing to use outdated versions that may contain known vulnerabilities.
The app does not use the recommended Android in-app update APIs, such as AppUpdateManager and AppUpdateInfo, to check for and request updates.
If an update mechanism exists, the app should handle failed or canceled update flows and retry or restrict access when forced updates are required.
If an immediate update flow is used, the app should check during onResume or other entry points whether a developer-triggered update is still in progress and resume it if necessary.
The app creates a Timer but never cancels it when the Activity is destroyed. This can keep references alive after the Activity lifecycle ends and cause a memory leak.

The app does not clean up long-running resources during the Activity lifecycle, such as calling cancelTimer() from onDestroy(). Missing lifecycle cleanup can lead to leaked Activity or Context references.

The scanner should identify common Android memory leak patterns, such as unregistered BroadcastReceivers, static Activity or View references, Singleton references to Context, inner class references, Handler references, AsyncTask references, Thread misuse, and TimerTask references.
If the app contains native code, the scanner should flag JNI, NDK, C, C++, or native library usage for further review of memory corruption risks.
If the app uses Java or Kotlin serialization/deserialization with untrusted data, the scanner should flag it for review because deserialization bugs can lead to security vulnerabilities.

Code/MASTG-TEST0044.title: Make Sure That Free Security Features Are Activated

expected_vulnerabilities.description: The app uses a native library compiled with stack canary protection disabled through -fno-stack-protector. Disabling stack smashing protection makes the native code more vulnerable to stack overflow attacks, which may lead to crashes or arbitrary code execution.
The app contains native code that should be checked for binary hardening protections. Native libraries should have security features such as stack canary and position-independent code enabled.
Native libraries should be compiled as position-independent code. If a native library has PIE or PIC disabled, address randomization protections may be weakened.

Because the app performs functionality through native code, the native library should be reviewed for memory corruption risks such as stack overflows, especially when compiler hardening protections are disabled.

Storage/MASTG-TEST0001.title: Testing Local Storage for Sensitive Data

expected_vulnerabilities.description: The app stores sensitive credentials or user-provided sensitive information in SharedPreferences. SharedPreferences should not be used for sensitive data unless the data is properly encrypted with securely managed keys.
The app requests WRITE_EXTERNAL_STORAGE permission, which can indicate that sensitive data may be written to external storage where it is more exposed to other apps or users.
The app encrypts a local database using a hardcoded key in the source code. Hardcoded cryptographic keys can be extracted from the app and used to decrypt locally stored sensitive data.
The app stores secret data in a local database. The database protection is insufficient because the encryption key is hardcoded, making the stored secrets recoverable.
The app adds a secret-like value in string.xml. Secrets stored in Android resources can be extracted from the APK and should not be treated as secure.

The app should avoid weak local encryption patterns such as XOR, bit flipping, encoded keys, or custom key hiding. Local encryption should rely on proven Android APIs and keys managed through Android Keystore.

Storage/MASTG-TEST0006.title: Determining Whether the Keyboard Cache Is Disabled for Text Input Fields

expected_vulnerabilities.description: The app contains sensitive login input fields where keyboard suggestions are not disabled. This may allow usernames, passwords, or other sensitive input to be cached or suggested by the keyboard.
Sensitive text input fields do not use android:inputType="textNoSuggestions" or an equivalent secure input type to prevent keyboard suggestions.

Password fields should use password-specific input types such as textPassword, textVisiblePassword, numberPassword, or textWebPassword. If password fields are plain text input fields, keyboard caching and visual exposure risks may increase.
The app should not overwrite secure XML input types in code with less secure values such as InputType.TYPE_CLASS_TEXT, because doing so can re-enable keyboard suggestions.
The app should ensure that the configured minimum SDK version supports the secure input type constants used for sensitive fields. Otherwise, the compiled app may not honor those constants.
The app leaves android:allowBackup="true" enabled in the AndroidManifest.xml file. If the app stores sensitive data locally, this may allow sensitive files to be included in device or cloud backups.
The app stores login and registration credentials in a local text file named credentials.txt using a plaintext format containing the username and password.

Because the app stores sensitive credentials locally while backup is enabled, the sensitive credentials may be included in Android Auto Backup or other backup mechanisms unless explicitly excluded or encrypted.
Sensitive files should be excluded from Android Auto Backup using backup rules, or encrypted before backup. If no backup exclusion configuration is present, sensitive local files may be backed up.
If the app defines a key/value backup agent, reviewers should inspect the BackupAgent or BackupAgentHelper implementation to determine whether sensitive data is backed up.
The app stores the encryption key as a String object in memory. Immutable objects such as String cannot be reliably overwritten, so sensitive values may remain in memory longer than necessary.
The app does not properly clear sensitive data from memory when the user signs out. Setting this.encryptionKey = null only removes the reference and does not overwrite the sensitive key material.
The app handles encrypted notes and may leave the encryption key or decrypted note content accessible in memory until the application is closed.

Sensitive values should be stored in mutable primitive arrays such as byte[] or char[] and overwritten when no longer needed. The app does not demonstrate proper overwrite-based cleanup for sensitive memory.

Highly sensitive information should be cleared when an Activity or Fragment enters onPause. If the app keeps sensitive notes or keys in memory across lifecycle transitions, the data may remain exposed.
